title: A robot, a cord and a narrow gap
lead: Researchers made puzzles that ask robots to turn parts or thread a cord. A team in Tokyo describes putting sensors on a robot hand so it can tell when a part catches.

news.title: A robot puzzle can start with a knot
news.summary: Northwestern University and its collaborators set up ninety puzzles for robots in a computer. The best program that wrote instructions for the robot solved about 43% of them in the standard test.
news.details: Researchers at Northwestern University and other organisations set ninety puzzles for robots in a computer. One asks a robot to move a piece through a narrow gap. Another asks it to thread a cord through a hole. The researchers wanted to see whether programs could guide the hands so that the pieces ended up in the right state.
news.technical_novelty: The puzzles cover assembly, untangling and narrow passages. The final state of the objects determines success.
news.engineering_impact: The two test settings give controllers different observations and different opportunities to restart.
news.limitations: The scores of about 43% and zero out of eighteen concern different systems and different sets of simulated puzzles.
news.evidence_status: Research preprint. The cited benchmark scores come from the authors’ simulation trials.
news.organization: Northwestern University, Microsoft, UC Berkeley and Carnegie Mellon University
news.body:
Researchers at Northwestern University and other organisations set ninety puzzles for robots in a computer. One asks a robot to move a piece through a narrow gap. Another asks it to thread a cord through a hole. The researchers wanted to see whether programs could guide the hands so that the pieces ended up in the right state.

Imagine trying to slide a wide object through an opening. Turning it sideways might make room, but only if there is space for the turn. A program has to choose such moves for the robot. The test checks where the pieces end up and how they fit together. The researchers made sure that each puzzle already had a solution that worked.

In the standard test, the best program that wrote instructions for the movements solved about 43% of the puzzles. Four other programs received pictures and a task to perform. Each faced eighteen puzzles designed for one arm, and none solved any of those eighteen in the computer test.

news.title: A robot hand can feel when a plug catches
news.summary: Tokyo’s XELA Robotics proposed using touch sensors when a robot puts a plug into a socket. It says sensors could also detect a small screw slipping between the fingers.
news.details: Tokyo-based XELA Robotics described how sensors on a robot hand could help guide a plug into a socket. When a plug is a little out of line, it might catch on the edge. A camera might not show the moment that happens. A touch sensor can measure how strongly the part pushes against the hand.
news.technical_novelty: Sensors on the hand measure contact and detect insertion resistance or signs of slipping.
news.engineering_impact: A controller can use the readings to reposition a connector or adjust the grip on a small part.
news.limitations: The release reports no damage rate or direct comparison with a camera-only system.
news.evidence_status: The sensor vendor described use cases and did not publish comparative test results.
news.body:
Tokyo-based XELA Robotics described how sensors on a robot hand could help guide a plug into a socket. When a plug is a little out of line, it might catch on the edge. A camera might not show the moment that happens. A touch sensor can measure how strongly the part pushes against the hand.

If the plug catches, the robot could change its position a little and try again. The program needs a signal telling it that the force has changed. The engineers proposed another use for the sensors: picking up a tiny screw without dropping it. Once the fingers close, they can hide the screw from the camera.

When the screw starts to slide, the sensors could report it before the screw falls. The program could then change how tightly the hand holds it. In one job the clue is a plug that pushes back, and in the other it is a screw that slips. The company described both ideas without giving a count of parts assembled without damage.

news.title: Two robots are going to learn warehouse work
news.summary: Logistics company Bleckmann bought two human-shaped robots for European warehouses. Once the machines arrive, workers plan to teach them jobs such as moving items and picking goods for orders.
news.details: On November 24, logistics company Bleckmann announced that it had invested in two human-shaped robots for European warehouses. It expects the machines to arrive in the coming weeks. Workers will then begin teaching them warehouse jobs. The company wants to find out how the robots learn to move things and pick goods for an order.
news.technical_novelty: The machines have cameras, laser distance sensors and software that builds a map while tracking their position.
news.engineering_impact: Bleckmann plans to collect data as it teaches the two machines to move items and pick orders.
news.limitations: The operator did not name the first sites or publish warehouse performance figures.
news.evidence_status: Operator announcement of the purchase and plans for training after delivery.
news.body:
On November 24, logistics company Bleckmann announced that it had invested in two human-shaped robots for European warehouses. It expects the machines to arrive in the coming weeks. Workers will then begin teaching them warehouse jobs. The company wants to find out how the robots learn to move things and pick goods for an order.

A box in a passage can change the route that a robot needs to take. Bleckmann says the machines use cameras and sensors that measure distance with a laser. Those measurements help software build a map and work out where the robot is. The company also describes a way to ask the robot to do a job using the human voice.

Workers plan to keep records of the jobs the two machines try. The records could help teach later robots. The company has not yet announced which warehouses will receive the first machines or how many orders they could pick in a shift.

news.title: What should workers check when a machine stops?
news.summary: Amada and Hitachi tested software that suggests checks when a machine has a problem. They also asked it to help rearrange work when an order deadline changes.
news.details: Two Japanese companies, Amada and Hitachi, tested a program that helps factory workers with two problems. Sometimes an order has to be ready sooner than expected. Sometimes a machine stops working. On November 26, the two companies explained what the program had been able to suggest in those situations.
news.technical_novelty: The assistant suggests changes after a deadline moves and proposes checks for a faulty machine.
news.engineering_impact: Amada and Hitachi plan to connect the assistant’s recommendations to equipment control.
news.limitations: The companies have yet to publish results from customer sites or measured repair times.
news.evidence_status: Joint company announcement of a proof of concept without quantitative results.
news.body:
Two Japanese companies, Amada and Hitachi, tested a program that helps factory workers with two problems. Sometimes an order has to be ready sooner than expected. Sometimes a machine stops working. On November 26, the two companies explained what the program had been able to suggest in those situations.

If a deadline moves up, a job planned for later in the day might have to happen in the morning. The program suggested changes to the schedule and ways to use the available machines. When a machine had a problem, it gave workers possible causes and a list of checks. For difficult cases, it could draw on knowledge collected during earlier repairs.

The companies plan to try the program at selected customer factories. They also want to build a connection that can pass a decision to a machine or robot. The test they described concerned advice. The companies did not report how many minutes that advice saved during a repair.

news.title: Could videos help teach a robot new moves?
news.summary: The team at Embo raised $110 million to work on software that teaches robots to move. It plans to learn from videos, records made by real machines and practice in computers.
news.details: On November 23, Embo said investors had put $110 million into its work on robot software. The team wants to teach a robot to choose a move when it faces an unfamiliar object. It plans to train the software with videos, records of real robots moving and exercises in computer models.
news.technical_novelty: Embo plans to learn from video predictions, robot motion records and computer practice.
news.engineering_impact: The training would connect predictions of what objects will do to choices about how a robot should move.
news.limitations: Embo has yet to publish success rates on unfamiliar tasks.
news.evidence_status: The company announced funding and a development plan. It did not publish controller performance.
news.body:
On November 23, Embo said investors had put $110 million into its work on robot software. The team wants to teach a robot to choose a move when it faces an unfamiliar object. It plans to train the software with videos, records of real robots moving and exercises in computer models.

A video can show what happens after a hand pushes a box. The team wants the program to look at the start of a video and learn to predict what happens next. Choosing a motion for a robot's own arm also calls for recordings from real robots. The developers plan to use those as a separate part of training.

The program would also get to practise in a computer. It would try a move and get feedback based on the result. If the box did not reach the target, the program could use that feedback to change how it chooses a move. Embo has described its plan and has yet to say how often a trained robot succeeds at a new task.

technology_signal.implications: The test checks where the objects end up and how they fit together. The scores describe the computer tests.
